history.heading: Island society
paragraphs: Palau, an archipelago of over 300 islands in the western Pacific, was settled around 3,000 years ago or more. Palauans developed a complex matrilineal society led by chiefs. Stone money used in Yap was quarried in Palau's Rock Islands.

Spain claimed Palau in the 19th century, sold it to Germany in 1899, and Japan ruled it from 1914, making Koror an administrative centre. The Battle of Peleliu in 1944 was among the bloodiest of the Pacific War.

history.heading: Independence
paragraphs: After the war Palau was part of the US-administered Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands. After several referendums, it became independent in 1994 under a Compact of Free Association with the United States.

culture.heading: Traditions
paragraphs: Palauan and English are official languages. Most people are Christian, and Modekngei, a local religion, is also practised. Traditional bai (meeting houses) are decorated with storyboards. Palau's Rock Islands Southern Lagoon is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and Jellyfish Lake is famous for its stingless jellyfish.

politics.heading: Presidential republic
paragraphs: Palau is a presidential republic with a bicameral national congress. Traditional chiefs also play a role. The US provides defence and funding under the Compact, renewed in 2024. Palau recognises Taiwan.

economy.heading: Tourism and conservation
paragraphs: Tourism, especially diving and snorkelling, is the main industry, alongside US aid and fishing. Palau created a national marine sanctuary covering 80 percent of its waters and requires visitors to sign a pledge to protect the environment. The currency is the US dollar.
